content: The diagnostic tools evaluated include GeneXpert, Truenat, and other cartridge-based point-of-care systems. These systems are used for drug susceptibility testing, specifically for detecting resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolones, and second-line injectable drugs. Searches for ongoing trials were conducted using government databases and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, with no language restrictions, up to September 6, 2020. An additional search was performed on November 4, 2020, using the terms Zeesan and MeltPro. Researchers from FIND, the WHO Global TB Programme, manufacturers, and other TB diagnostic experts were contacted for information on unpublished or ongoing studies. Data submitted in response to the WHO public call were also reviewed. Drug resistance was assessed against a phenotypic reference standard (or a genotypic reference standard for ethionamide resistance) and a composite reference standard combining phenotypic and genotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) results from studies where both methods were performed. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, which provides an overall quality assessment and a framework for translating evidence into recommendations. In the GRADE system, diagnostic accuracy studies, despite being observational, are initially considered high-quality evidence. The GRADEpro Guideline Development Tool software was used to generate summary tables of findings. Evidence quality was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on five factors: risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and other considerations. Evidence was downgraded by one level for serious issues and by two levels for very serious issues in any of these factors. PICO 1: Isoniazid Resistance Detection Three multinational studies involving 1,605 participants provided data for evaluating isoniazid resistance detection. The reference standard for these studies was culture-based phenotypic DST. Each study center was analyzed as a separate study. Concerns were raised about indirectness in the study populations, as the prevalence of isoniazid resistance in some settings was higher than global estimates, limiting applicability to lower-prevalence settings. Additionally, mutations in isoniazid monoresistant strains appeared more diverse than those in multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains. Most participants in the included studies had rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB), despite the PICO question being irrespective of rifampicin resistance. Consequently, evidence certainty was downgraded one level for indirectness, and the quality of evidence was rated as moderate for both sensitivity and specificity. Sensitivity ranged from 81% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 87% to 100%. PICO 2: Fluoroquinolone Resistance Detection Three multinational studies with 1,337 participants provided data for evaluating fluoroquinolone resistance detection. The reference standard was culture-based phenotypic DST. Each study center was analyzed separately. Specificity estimates were inconsistent, ranging from 84% to over 96%, and the heterogeneity could not be explained. As a result, evidence certainty was downgraded one level for inconsistency. The quality of evidence was rated as high for sensitivity and moderate for specificity. Sensitivity ranged from 83% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 84% to 100%. PICO 3: Ethionamide Resistance Detection One multinational study with 434 participants provided data for evaluating ethionamide resistance. The reference standard was DNA sequencing of the inhA promoter. Each study center was analyzed separately. Evidence certainty was downgraded two levels for risk of bias due to the limited number of participants and the wide confidence intervals for sensitivity and specificity. The quality of evidence was rated as very low for both sensitivity and specificity. Sensitivity ranged from 78% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 97% to 100%. PICO 4: Amikacin Resistance Detection One multinational study with 490 participants provided data for evaluating amikacin resistance. The reference standard was culture-based phenotypic DST. Each study center was analyzed separately. The 95% confidence intervals for sensitivity were wide, leading to potential variability in decision-making regarding true positives and false negatives. Additionally, there were few participants with amikacin resistance contributing to the sensitivity analysis. Evidence certainty was downgraded two levels for imprecision. The quality of evidence was rated as low for sensitivity and high for specificity. Sensitivity ranged from 75% to 95%, and specificity ranged from 96% to 100%. Cost-Effectiveness Analysis A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the cost, affordability, and cost-effectiveness of implementing low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Four databases (Embase, Medline, Web of Science, and Scopus) were searched for studies published between January 1, 2010, and September 17, 2020. Experts and manufacturers were contacted to identify unpublished studies. Two low-complexity automated NAATs were identified: MeltPro MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/XDR. Only data concerning Xpert MTB/XDR were included in this review. The Xpert MTB/XDR assay can test unprocessed or concentrated sputum and provides results in less than 90 minutes. However, no published studies directly assessed the cost or cost-effectiveness of this assay. The test cartridge costs $80 ex-works, with additional costs for shipping, customs, and equipment upgrades. The Xpert MTB/XDR test requires 10-color GeneXpert modules, necessitating laboratory upgrades. Upgrade options include purchasing new 10-color systems, adding satellite instruments, or converting existing systems, with costs ranging from $3,860 to $72,350 depending on the option chosen. Additional costs may arise from repeated testing in cases of indeterminate or invalid results. The cost-effectiveness of Xpert MTB/XDR depends on diagnostic accuracy, placement within diagnostic algorithms, and the local standard of care. Faster time to results may improve treatment initiation, reduce loss to follow-up, and improve survival rates. However, the high costs associated with extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB treatment are a significant driver of overall costs. Identifying more XDR-positive individuals requiring treatment will increase total resource requirements. Long-term population-level impacts, such as reduced transmission, require further investigation through transmission modeling. In summary, while the Xpert MTB/XDR assay offers rapid results and potential benefits for TB management, its cost-effectiveness remains uncertain due to limited direct evidence and the high costs associated with implementation and treatment.
